transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Integrated risk prediction, for Thursday, November 26.
Let's turn to integrated risk prediction, where genetic scores are combined with other kinds of data.

The first paper comes from the Mirzaei lab, in the British Journal of Nutrition. The question was whether a three-SNP genetic risk score interacts with a lifestyle risk score to affect cardiometabolic markers and lifetime risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
And the cohort is small. It's two hundred fifty-six Iranian women with overweight or obesity, so this is clearly exploratory work.

Right, and the outcome reflects that. Some of the gene-by-lifestyle interactions were nominally significant, but none survived Bonferroni correction. The authors themselves call for replication in larger cohorts.
A three-variant score also captures only a small part of polygenic risk. So I'd treat this as a starting point for building hypotheses, not as evidence that the interaction is real.
The second paper is at the opposite end on scale. It's from the Plym lab in JAMA Network Open, and it uses fifty-nine thousand and sixty-seven men from the Stockholm3 prostate cancer screening trial.
They asked whether genetic risk adds to PSA for long-term prostate cancer risk. They grouped men by baseline PSA, family history and a two-hundred-thirty-two-variant polygenic risk score.

Among men with a PSA of one nanogram per milliliter or higher, the top polygenic score quintile roughly tripled the ten-year risk of clinically significant cancer. It was also linked to higher prostate cancer mortality, with a hazard ratio of two point seven one.
That supports layering genetics on top of PSA-based screening. One caution is that this is a Swedish screening population, so how well it transfers to other ancestries still needs testing.
Put side by side, the two papers show how much sample size and score breadth matter when you're looking for added value from genetics.
The takeaway is that well-powered polygenic scores can add real risk information to clinical markers like PSA, while small studies of gene-by-lifestyle interaction still need replication.

papers.title: Interaction between 3-SNP genetic risk score and lifestyle risk score on cardiovascular risk factors and the risk of lifetime ASCVD among overweight and obese women
